summary: Undefined behavior (UB) means the C standard places no requirements on what happens. The program may crash, print garbage, appear to work, or be silently miscompiled, because the compiler is allowed to assume UB never occurs.

sections.heading: Three kinds of unpredictable
bullets: Undefined behavior: no requirements at all (null dereference, signed overflow).
Unspecified behavior: the implementation picks among allowed options and need not document it (order of evaluating function arguments).
Implementation-defined behavior: the compiler must document its choice (size of int, right shift of negative numbers).

sections.heading: Common sources
bullets: Signed integer overflow: `INT_MAX + 1`.
Division by zero.
Out-of-bounds array access or pointer arithmetic.
Dereferencing NULL or dangling pointers.
Reading an uninitialized automatic variable.
Modifying a string literal.
Modifying a variable twice between sequence points: `i = i++ + ++i`.
Strict-aliasing violations and misaligned access.
Shifting by a negative or too-large amount.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.code:
int a = INT_MAX; a + 1;          // signed overflow: UB
int arr[4]; arr[5] = 0;          // out of bounds: UB
int *p = NULL; *p = 1;           // null deref: UB
char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'x';    // string literal write: UB
int i = 4; int r = i++ * i++;    // unsequenced: UB

sections.heading: Why the standard allows it
sections.body: Leaving behavior undefined lets compilers skip bounds and overflow checks and optimize aggressively. Signed overflow being UB lets `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)` be assumed to terminate and be vectorized. The price is that bugs may not fail where they occur.

sections.heading: Consequences
bullets: Results differ across compilers, versions, and optimization levels.
Optimizers can delete checks that rely on UB, e.g. `if (x + 1 < x)` is removed for signed x.
Security holes: many exploits start as UB.
Debugging is hard because failures appear far from the cause.

sections.body: Unsigned arithmetic is specified to wrap, so `UINT_MAX + 1 == 0` is fine. Signed overflow is not. Prefer unsigned types for bit manipulation and check ranges before signed arithmetic.
sections.code:
if (a > INT_MAX - b) { /* would overflow */ }
else sum = a + b;

sections.body: Between two sequence points an object may be modified at most once, and its prior value may be read only to compute the new value. `a[i] = i++` and `printf("%d %d", i++, i++)` violate this. Split such statements.

subtopics.title: Strict aliasing
subtopics.summary: Accessing an object through the wrong type.

sections.body: Reading a `float` through an `int *` is UB, letting compilers reorder or drop loads. To reinterpret bytes safely use `memcpy` or a `union` as documented by your compiler.
sections.code:
float f = 1.0f; uint32_t u;
memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u);   // safe

sections.body: Build with `-fsanitize=undefined,address -Wall -Wextra`. UBSan reports signed overflow, bad shifts, null deref, and misaligned access at run time. Static analyzers and `-O2` warnings catch more, and tools like Frama-C or CompCert's interpreter define behavior exactly.

Because the compiler may assume UB never happens it can skip bounds and overflow checks, keep values in registers wider than their declared type, and reorder or vectorize loops. This is why signed overflow is undefined while unsigned wraps: the freedom is a deliberate trade for speed.

bullets: Passing NULL to printf's `%s`.
Calling realloc with a size of 0 (implementation-defined or UB depending on version).
Using a pointer after realloc moved the block.
Comparing or subtracting pointers to different arrays.
In C++: `delete this`, deleting through a base pointer without a virtual destructor.

takeaways: UB gives the compiler license to assume it never happens.
Signed overflow, out-of-bounds, null deref, uninitialized reads, and unsequenced modifications are UB.
Unspecified and implementation-defined are different from undefined.
Use -fsanitize=undefined and clean warnings to catch it.
